analysis.one_liner: Requires insurers to sell and renew coverage regardless of health, caps age-based premiums, and sets standard benefits and billing rules.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to four House committees and never received a vote or a hearing before the 104th Congress ended in January 1997.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have forced health insurers to sell coverage to anyone who applied and to keep renewing it, no matter their health history. It would have limited preexisting-condition exclusions to six months (with credit for prior coverage), capped how much more insurers could charge older customers, required a standard benefit package with free preventive care, and let parents keep children on family plans until age 26. It also set uniform electronic billing standards and barred small employers from self-insuring, routing that business through regulated carriers.
analysis.who_benefits: People with preexisting conditions who could be denied or priced out of coverage; individual buyers and small employers in the individual and small-group markets; families with young adult children up to age 26; and patients who would gain required coverage of mammograms, cancer screenings, prenatal care, clinical-trial costs, and off-label drugs. Insurers could no longer deny, cancel, or refuse to renew coverage except for nonpayment or fraud.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with preexisting conditions and small employers

how_it_helps.text: Requires every carrier in the individual and small-group market to accept every small employer and qualifying individual who applies, and to renew coverage except for nonpayment, fraud, or a full market exit with notice.

Limits preexisting-condition exclusions to six months and requires credit of one month for each month of prior continuous coverage; pregnancy, newborns, and adopted children are exempted from exclusions entirely.
Restricts premium variation to age, geography, family size, benefit design, and expense category, and phases the highest-to-lowest age rate ratio down to 3-to-1 by 2000.

Requires standard coverage to include preventive benefits with no cost sharing (well-child care, mammograms, pap smears, colorectal and prostate screening, immunizations, prenatal care) and coverage of routine costs in approved clinical trials and compendia-listed off-label drugs.
Requires an option under which children under 26 are treated as family members for coverage purposes.

Bars carriers from paying agents or brokers more for enrolling healthier people, and imposes a $100-per-day tax on carriers for each person affected by a compliance failure, with Labor Department enforcement over group plans.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and managed care organizations bear the cost: they lose the ability to screen out or price out sick applicants, face standard benefit packages, disclosure rules, agent-compensation limits, a per-day excise tax for noncompliance, and a five-year ban on re-entering a market they exit. Healthy and younger enrollees could see higher premiums as community rating spreads costs across the pool, though the bill builds in a risk-adjustment system to offset that.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

drawbacks.text: Guaranteed issue with tightly limited rating can push premiums up for younger, healthier buyers if sick people enroll in disproportionate numbers; the bill tries to manage this with a mandated state risk-adjustment system but does not eliminate the effect.

The bill preempts state laws restricting managed care: states could no longer prohibit network plans from limiting covered providers, requiring referrals (except for obstetrics and gynecology), restricting the number of participating providers, or negotiating payment rates, which narrows state-level consumer protections.

High-deductible coverage may be sold only to people who show they hold assets at least equal to the deductible, and carriers may not offer cheaper, skinnier plans below that floor, limiting options for people with little savings.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections (guaranteed issue and renewal, six-month cap on preexisting-condition exclusions, 3-to-1 age rating, free preventive care, coverage to age 26) would have materially helped people the individual and small-group market failed, at a real cost to insurers' underwriting freedom and possibly to premiums for healthy enrollees, which the risk-adjustment system was designed to blunt. The managed-care preemption in Sec. 111(e) is the serious good-faith objection: it trades away some state consumer protections as part of the package.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to four House committees at once, then split among four subcommittees, none of which ever reported it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Peterson of Florida introduced the bill on March 20, 1996, with 49 original cosponsors; it drew 54 total cosponsors (52 Democrats and 2 independents).
The House referred it to four committees at once: Commerce, Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Economic and Educational Opportunities, with consideration timing left to be determined by the Speaker.
Between March 26 and April 10, 1996, it was further referred to four subcommittees: Health, Commerce Trade and Hazardous Materials, Health and Environment, and Employer-Employee Relations.
No committee reported the bill, no floor vote ever occurred, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 with the bill still in committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and managed care plans are better off because the bill died: they avoided guaranteed issue, a 3-to-1 cap on age rating, standardized benefit packages, agent-compensation limits, and a $100-per-day excise tax for noncompliance. People with preexisting conditions and small employers did not get these protections from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers and managed care plans

for.name: Rep. Pete Peterson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Health Insurance Affordability Act of 1996 and assembled 49 original cosponsors.

for.name: 52 of 204 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 52 Democratic backers including members from both the progressive and conservative wings of the caucus.

for.name: 2 Independent representatives
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Rep. Bernard Sanders of Vermont.

against.name: Speaker Newt Gingrich
against.what_they_did: The House referred the bill to four committees simultaneously, with the timing of consideration left to the Speaker's subsequent determination, a path that requires every committee to act before the bill can move.

against.name: Thomas Bliley
against.role: Chair, House Commerce Committee (majority committee of referral)
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill and its Health and Health and Environment subcommittees held it; the committee never reported the bill or held a vote on it.

against.name: Bill Archer
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill for its tax and ERISA provisions and never reported it.

against.name: Henry Hyde
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill for its antitrust title and never reported it.

against.name: Bill Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Economic and Educational Opportunities Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill for its employer-plan provisions and its Employer-Employee Relations subcommittee held it without action.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever taken; every cosponsor was a Democrat or independent, and the Republican-controlled committees to which the bill was referred never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would strip insurers' ability to deny, cancel, or price out sick customers, cap age rating at 3-to-1, impose a $100-per-day compliance tax, and penalize market exits with a five-year re-entry ban. At the same time it would bar employers with fewer than 100 employees from self-insuring, routing more of the small-group market through regulated carriers, and Title II's standardized electronic transactions would create uniform rules for the industry's billing infrastructure.

Sec. 111(e) would preempt state laws that restrict managed care practices (limiting provider networks, requiring referrals, and negotiating rates), a significant win for HMOs, while guaranteed-issue, disclosure, and network due-process rules would impose new obligations on them.

industries.industry: Health claims processing and health information services
industries.note: Title II would mandate uniform electronic data standards, unique identifiers, and network privacy standards for health transactions, creating a defined market for entities that process and transmit standard-format health information.

The bill would prohibit carriers from varying agent and broker compensation based on the health status or claims experience of the people they enroll, removing a financial incentive to cherry-pick healthy customers.
